item.title: Are We Beginning to Sound Like the Chatbots We Talk To?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Are We Beginning to Sound Like the Chatbots We Talk To?

The language used by chatbots and by humans may be converging.

Posted September 8, 2026

Key points
  • AI “tells” include em dashes, Oxford commas, negative parallelisms, and trending vocabulary.
  • Brief chatbot interactions can cause users to mimic AI language in later conversations.
  • Bidirectional influence means human and AI language may over time become virtually indistinguishable.
Changes in chatbot and human language may be bidirectional
Source: OpenAI / ChatGPT

A study released last month by the Pew Research Center was designed to answer an intriguing question: How much of the internet’s content is being generated by artificial intelligence?

The Pew researchers randomly selected 10,000 web pages to study. All of these had been written in English and published online during the past five years. The content of these pages was analyzed with Open Pangram, a widely used AI detection tool.

The results are sobering. Fully 10 percent of the webpages showed “significant signs of AI authorship.” And when the researchers filtered out the older pages, created before the release of ChatGPT in late 2022, the pattern was even more pronounced: 35 percent of the more recent pages—more than one-third—showed signs of having been artificially generated.

Linguistic tells

What sorts of cues suggest that a given text was generated by AI?

The Pew study’s authors point out that a great deal of the text used to train large language models (LLMs), like the one that underlies ChatGPT, consists of academic and journalistic writing. As a result, the output of AI-generated text is biased towards a more formal type of prose.

Specifically, the Pew researchers identified four characteristics that are common across AI-generated texts. These features can function like the “tells” of a novice poker player, who gives away the fact that they’ve been dealt a winning hand. For this analysis, the researchers examined 490,000 web pages to identify linguistic changes that have taken place since 2023.

The tells for AI-generated texts include em dashes—like these—and the use of Oxford commas, in which punctuation appears after the second-to-last item in a series (as with the comma after “writing” in “Children are taught reading, writing, and arithmetic in school”). In addition, AI-generated text contains a greater number of negative parallelisms. These are constructions like “It’s not a bug, it’s a feature.”

The final tell has to do with vocabulary. The researchers identified nearly 30 words and phrases that have “more than doubled in usage” since 2023. Examples include crucial, enhance, garner, intricate, meticulous, significant, and tapestry.

The findings seem clear enough, but how should they be interpreted? One might conclude that AI-generated language is rapidly taking over the online world. However, the Pew study is correlational, so cause and effect can’t be determined. In fact, the reverse may be true: It could be that the way people speak and write is being influenced by exposure to chatbots.

Drivers of linguistic change

Why might this be happening—after all, who wants to sound like a chatbot?

Think, for a moment, about how slang or colloquial expressions propagate from speaker to speaker. A good example would be the phrase “six seven,” which spread virally on TikTok about a year ago and was embraced enthusiastically by Gen Alpha speakers.

People may consciously adopt certain ways of speaking because they’re in vogue. But these changes can also take place outside of conscious awareness. This phenomenon, long studied by language researchers, is referred to as lexical entrainment. Simply put, we start sounding like others with whom we spend a lot of time, such as friends, classmates, or coworkers. And this may now include the time we spend interacting with chatbots.

Researchers have documented that this seems to be happening. Hiromu Yakura and his colleagues at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development analyzed over 730,000 hours of conversation, drawn from more than 820,000 podcast episodes. Since most of these interactions are unscripted, podcasts give researchers an excellent opportunity to see whether extemporaneous spoken language is undergoing any sort of linguistic shift.

The changes documented by Yakura's team are remarkably similar to those from the Pew study. They identified 20 words, preferentially used by ChatGPT, that have “increased abruptly in spontaneous human speech.” Their list includes a quarter of the terms that were identified by the Pew researchers: boast, bolster, delve, intricate, meticulous, showcase, and underscore.

Determining cause and effect

Yakura’s results are intriguing, but they are still correlational, so cause and effect can’t be disentangled.

However, these researchers also conducted an experiment in which “a brief chatbot interaction led research participants to adopt its words as their own." This mimicking behavior persisted in a subsequent task, when the participants were asked to describe a series of images. Because the behavioral change was observed experimentally, the direction of the effect can be identified: The bots were influencing the speech used by humans.

A couple of caveats, however, should be kept in mind. One is that Yakura’s study has not yet been published, so the methodology and results have not been subjected to peer review.

Another qualification is that this process of entrainment may have already peaked. Both studies found that lexical entrainment increased rapidly from 2023 to mid-2024 but has been holding steady or even declining somewhat since then.

It may be that, as certain terms become “tainted” in the popular imagination—and the word delve may be the poster child here—people might consciously alter their word choices to avoid terms strongly associated with chatbot-speak.

It should also be kept in mind that the LLMs are changing too. Companies like OpenAI and Anthropic release new and improved versions every few weeks. These newer iterations are trained on more recent texts that reflect the linguistic shifts already taking place in human speech. Due to this bidirectional effect, it may become virtually impossible, over time, to distinguish between human and AI-generated language.

item.title: Stuck in a Relationship Rut?
item.description:
Relationships

Stuck in a Relationship Rut?

Curiosity about your mate can help combat relationship habituation.

Posted September 8, 2026

Key points
  • Many couples experience phases in which they feel stuck in a rut or bored in their relationship.
  • Although common, relationship habituation can leave many feeling uninspired and disconnected.
  • Staying curious about how your mate is evolving and growing over time can help couples grow in parallel.
Source: Mixmike/Getty Images Signature

When people find that special someone and commit to a long-term relationship, they often think their future is bright, that they know their mate. They choose them—and the rest of life will unfold into a happy, fulfilled, easy existence.

Over time, romantic relationships can sometimes fall into boring, stagnant, or uninspired phases in which people feel like they are “going through the motions” of life without any newness. Relationship habituation generally describes when couples become stagnant, stuck in a rut that can feel boring and predictable. In essence, relationships can fall stale and fail to inspire growth because we fall into patterns that neglect growth and change.

Of course, it’s easy to let this happen. As we age, our responsibilities in daily life accumulate, and people neglect to connect with their mate because of competing interests or obligations. For example, early in romantic relationships, the mate is often the first priority and garners great attention, time, and effort. Yet, over time, other competing interests like parenting kids, work responsibilities, and even self-care may come before the partner.

Getting Curious About Your Mate

As anyone who has been in a lasting romantic relationship knows, the journey of life is full of change. We want to grow in parallel with our mate over time if our relationship is going to last. This means that we need to learn about how they are changing—things like what they are learning, what new passions they develop, what preoccupies their mind—over the course of time. In essence, we need to stay curious about who they were, who they are now, and who they are becoming.

Research suggests that interpersonal curiosity, or the desire to authentically understand a mate or another person, generally increases feelings of trust and psychological safety, encourages vulnerability and sharing, builds attachment/bonding, promotes empathy, and helps partners stay connected through difficult times (Jauniaux & Lawford, 2024). It can create a safe but interesting and engaging space for couples to continue to connect as they evolve and grow over time (Aron et al., 2020).

Inspiring Curiosity Through Conversation

So, how can you spark a newfound curiosity in a long-term relationship? Engaging in open-ended, exploratory conversations with your mate is key. There are no “bad questions,” as long as they are asked authentically in a nonjudgmental way to understand your mate.

The easiest topics for many people to explore about everyday preferences and experiences give rise to questions like:

  • What was the best part of your day today?
  • The hardest part?
  • Do you have any regrets about how you handled something today?
  • What made you smile? What surprised you? Disappointed you?
  • What is occupying your mind?

For more of a challenge, expand conversations to include larger life values and priorities that are deeper but also require more vulnerability. Questions like:

  • If you could do anything, what would your ideal day look like? Who would be there? How could I help make it exceptional?
  • What are you focused on in the coming year? What is on your bucket list?
  • What’s something that’s changed about you in the last year? Five years?
  • What gives your life purpose or meaning?
  • What is a current world issue that you are struggling with understanding or conflicted about? Why?
  • What matters to you most in life, and how do you express that?

The hardest conversations often center around your relationship. Questions like:

  • What is different about being married to me than you expected?
  • What do you appreciate the most about me as a partner?
  • What is something you’d like me to work on?
  • What do you wish I understood about you?
  • What is most difficult for you when we fight?
  • How can I be a better mate to you?
  • What do you need to be more fulfilled in this relationship?
  • How can we grow together and not drift apart?

The Naked Truth

When couples stop trying to explore themselves and their mate, or stop getting curious about who they and their partner are becoming over time, it is much easier to disconnect from each other. Developing a mindset that sparks curiosity about your mate helps couples stay excited, connected, and interested in one another over time.

Of course, there are ways to make this negative. If conversations feel accusatory or blaming, they will not build curiosity because a person will become less likely to share. If the information is being gathered to be used against them (e.g., “You said you were jealous, so now I can’t trust you with my deepest fantasies”), to punish them, or to control/manipulate them, it is not a safe space to be curious together. That said, if your relationship is feeling stuck, start asking questions! Maybe lead simply with that statement: “I’m feeling a little uninspired in our life right now—it feels too regimented, and I’d like to talk to you about that.” See where the conversation leads you.

Copyright Cortney S. Warren, Ph.D., ABPP

Note: This content is only for informational and educational purposes and should not be considered therapy or any form of treatment. I cannot respond to personal requests for advice over the internet. Best wishes on your continued journey.

item.title: Choosing Yourself Can Strengthen Bonds With Others
item.description:
Relationships

Choosing Yourself Can Strengthen Bonds With Others

How we treat ourselves is what we bring to our relationships.

Posted September 8, 2026

Key points
  • Choosing yourself means giving yourself attention and honoring your needs.
  • Self-neglect often hides behind helping others and can lead to burnout and confusion.
  • When we choose ourselves, our relationships can improve because we're modeling self-worth.
Source: Toni Vans/Unsplash

When I hear clients say they feel lost in their significant relationships, I get more confused looks when I reply, “You might consider choosing yourself.” Self-neglect, or not choosing yourself, is an insidious dynamic, often camouflaged by hard work and helping others. Before exploring what choosing yourself actually is, it might be helpful to say what it’s not. It isn’t excessive narcissism, which is the desperate search for the self, an obsession with acquiring a valued sense of self.

What Choosing Yourself Looks Like

Choosing yourself is similar to choosing anything. Here are some characteristics of choosing ourselves.

  • Worth your attention. Like most things we choose, when we choose ourselves, we believe we are worth our attention.
  • Attending. Several aspects of our character are waiting for our attention. We can consider our emotions by feeling them, naming them, and talking about them. Needs and desires also wait to be realized. We also create stories about ourselves, others, places, and things. There are actions to consider.
  • Allow attention to generate intention. When we give ourselves attention, we begin to intend some form of action that we likely believe will benefit us.

Signs That You're Not Choosing Yourself

Some degree of self-neglect is inevitable, especially when parenting young children or building a career. The hope is that we don’t lose so much connection with ourselves that we develop a medical condition or lose someone we love. We can experience the following signs of not choosing ourselves.

  • Burnout. Severe self-neglect can deplete energy and be accompanied by poor sleep and poor nutrition.
  • Confusion. It’s easy to lack clarity about what you need and want, and what will truly serve you.
  • Blame. It can be easy to hold others responsible when we feel expended.
  • A tendency to be impetuous. We can overreact as we try to show confidence when we actually feel insecure.

Choosing Yourself and Being Chosen by Others

I recently worked with George, a 48-year-old entrepreneur who felt neither chosen by his wife nor by his children. It became clear that George expected his family to choose him instead of choosing himself. He began to identify ways in which he did not choose himself. The list included diet, sleep, exercise, dental check-ups, time with friends, and not making business contacts that would likely support his work. Finally, he took responsibility for choosing himself personally and professionally. Soon, George reported that his wife seemed more affectionate and his teenage sons wanted to spend time with him.

Essentially, George was communicating: “I’m worth my own attention and yours.” He experienced renewed respect and involvement. He communicated to his family that he was primarily responsible for choosing himself. He put responsibility in the right place, alleviating others from having to save him.

George’s story is a good example of how much building relationships with others is an inside job. Choosing ourselves is one of the only aspects of relationships that is in our control. How we treat ourselves as we relate to others is what we bring to the relationship. Our presence can be an invitation to joy, peace, and kindness, or a message that we don’t deserve such things. It doesn’t mean we need to remain on top of the world; it’s only about being honest when we feel stuck. The key is that we’re responsible for choosing ourselves, and that may require asking for help. Also, we don’t fall into excessive people-pleasing as a nonverbal contract that makes the other person responsible for choosing us. We simply commit to do our best, not to abdicate our responsibility, and to choose ourselves.

item.title: How to Be the Author of Your Own Life in the Age of AI
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

How to Be the Author of Your Own Life in the Age of AI

Martin Seligman on the power of agency in the AI era.

Posted September 8, 2026

Martin Seligman, PhD, is widely regarded as the father of positive psychology, making groundbreaking discoveries in the field over the course of his rich and impactful career. As artificial intelligence (AI) takes the world by storm, Seligman’s body of work illuminates AI’s potential to significantly contribute to human progress as we’ve never before experienced, or to steal the very thing that drives humans forward, individually and collectively: agency.

Seligman’s latest book, Agency: The Psychological History of Human Progress, offers readers an in-depth look into the role agency has played in the advancement of humanity over the course of history, and how we can build our capacity for agency today.

Martin Seligman is widely regarded as the father of positive psychology.
Source: Mandy Seligman/Used with permission

Q: Share a bit about your background and what inspired you to write Agency.

Martin Seligman: In 1964, I watched an animal that had been given shocks it could not control lie down and take the next shock, even after the door to safety was left standing wide open. We called it learned helplessness, and it soon turned out that people do exactly the same thing. That single observation set the course of the next 60 years of my life, first through the study of depression and pessimism, the dark version of the phenomenon, and then through its mirror image, learned optimism, resilience, and the founding of positive psychology.

For decades I was circling something I could not yet name. Late in the arc it finally came clear. Beneath helplessness and optimism alike lay one underlying dimension, and I called it agency: the conviction, and the capacity, that what you do makes a difference, that you are the author of your own life and not a spectator to it. What turned the idea into a book was a discovery I never saw coming.

I set out to measure agency in the actual written record of humanity, millions of words across 3,000 years and a dozen civilizations. What I found stopped me cold. Agency is not a fixed feature of human nature. It flares up at particular moments in history, and wherever it rises, an explosion of human progress follows close behind. Where it collapses, whole civilizations stall. Agency, I became convinced, is the hidden engine of progress, and we have never needed to understand it more than we do right now.

Q: How do you define agency, and how can readers cultivate it in their own lives?

MS: Agency has three parts, and the good news is that you can build every one of them. The first is efficacy, the belief that your actions can actually move the world in front of you right now. The second is optimism, the belief that you can reach your goals down the road, sometimes very far down the road. The third is imagination, the power to picture a future that does not yet exist and to see the path that gets you there. Put the three together and you have a person who envisions a better world, expects to bring it about, and acts. Take any one away and the whole engine stalls.

None of this is fixed at birth. Efficacy is rebuilt the very way helplessness is reversed, by taking small, controllable actions and letting yourself notice, really notice, that your own effort changed the result. Optimism can be learned. We teach people to catch their catastrophic thoughts in the act, to argue with them the way you would argue with an unfair rival, and to find the more accurate and more hopeful reading of events. Imagination grows through prospection, the deeply human habit of traveling into the future in your mind, trying on possibilities, and rehearsing the plan.

Here is the line I most want readers to carry out of the book: The people who flourish are not the ones to whom good things happen. They are the ones with a hand on the tiller.

Source: Simon and Schuster/Used with permission

Q: In a time when artificial intelligence (AI) is being promoted as the future of societal progress, what have you discovered about the role of personal agency in human advancement?

MS: Here is what the record showed, and it is not what I expected. In the oldest texts, human beings are essentially puppets. Before roughly 1000 B.C.E., the gods command and mortals obey, and for century after century almost nothing changes. Then the needle jumps. In Persia, the language of human will multiplies nearly fivefold between the old hymns and the new. Across the world, in the narrow window we now call the Axial Age, people suddenly begin to speak as the authors of their own fate, and within a few generations you get the pre-Socratic philosophers, the Hebrew prophets, the Buddha, and Confucius. Progress does not march in step with intelligence. It marches in step with agency.

That is the finding that matters for our moment. No innovation in history has ever come from intelligence sitting on a shelf. It comes from human beings who believed the future was theirs to shape, and who then picked up whatever tools they had and shaped it. Artificial intelligence is one of those tools, the most powerful we have ever built, and like every tool before it, it is inert without agentic people to wield it. So the real question about the future is not how smart our machines become. It is whether we remain the authors of what those machines are for.

Q: With significant debate taking place the world over regarding the ethics and long-term societal value of AI, what is your take on AI in light of psychological agency and the history of human progress?

MS: I am an optimist about AI. My own history of agency was only possible because these tools let us read and measure the entire written inheritance of humanity at a scale no team of scholars could ever match. That is the good future, and it is a genuinely thrilling one.

There is also a bad future, and it is the one that keeps me up at night, because I have spent my life studying it under another name. If we hand our decisions, our judgments, and our very sense of authorship over to our machines, we will have engineered learned helplessness on a civilizational scale. The danger was never that AI becomes too powerful. The danger is that we become too passive, comfortable spectators to a future that something else has chosen for us.

We are living at a hinge moment. The choice of whether to remain the authors of our own lives, and of the future we share, is being made right now, by each of us alone and by all of us together. My deepest hope is that a reader closes the book not with a theory but with a decision: to keep a hand on the tiller and to realize the future is theirs to shape. Because the most remarkable finding of a lifetime of research is exactly this: When we believe the future is up to us, it is.

item.title: Yes, You Too Can Fall for a Scam
item.description:
Decision-Making

Yes, You Too Can Fall for a Scam

Scammers bypass your intelligence by targeting your emotions and trust.

Posted September 8, 2026

Key points
  • Anyone can fall for a scam. Scammers rely on urgency and scare tactics to bypass your usual sense of caution.
  • Your social media can give scammers a way to target you.
  • Pause before reacting; use encryption, blocking, and two-factor authentication; limit "training" on AI.
Falling for a scam can be devastating.
Source: Vitaly Gariev/Pexels

All last week, I felt stupid and ashamed for being duped by a scam. I’d had an ugly argument with someone I love, and it left me demoralized and not sleeping well. So, when an email hit my inbox from Microsoft saying my subscription had been upgraded to “Premium Class,” and my credit card had been charged an extra $397, it upset me, and I took the bait.

Usually when I get unsolicited or suspicious emails, I flag them, categorize them as scams, and report them. I’m a publicized author. My name, photos, and videos are out there, making me vulnerable to scams, some directly targeting authors, some targeting anyone with a bank account. Romance scammers send me praise on my writing and ask me to follow them. Delete, block, flag. That’s my usual response.

But this time, I fell. If I were being charged for something I didn’t order, I wanted to correct it right now. Without stopping to think, I impulsively called the Microsoft number in the email. Had I been in my usual security-vigilant frame of mind, I wouldn’t have called. I would have loaded Microsoft.com into my browser, accessed my account that way, and checked it.

When a man answered my call, a long conversation began in which he engaged me in a very tedious procedure to correct the erroneous charge. Eventually my call was “elevated” to a senior officer who said he was an FBI agent. He sent me a photo of himself over an image of his badge number. The two men were able to look at my bank accounts before alarm bells finally went off in my head, and I ended the call.

I was lucky I came to my senses in time, but the damage was burdensome—close those bank accounts, start new ones, destroy current checks, shore up online security, contact autopay accounts with new bank account numbers. I had to verify that credit reporting agencies indeed had retained a freeze on my accounts, which I had put in place after a credit card of mine was hacked last year. The list goes on.

How Could I Have Been So Stupid?

Stressed and angry at myself, I’ve done some research on why someone as careful as I am takes the bait even once. According to the University of Central Florida, there are three main factors:

  1. Hackers target human emotions. They do their best to engender fear in the victim or a sense of urgency to fix a problem. They gamble on the human need to trust others.
  2. There is a situational vulnerability in the victim—the death of a loved one, a new job, information overload (e.g., a busy lifestyle with a constant stream of data to monitor).
  3. Tech or social factors: Scammers try to trick you into handing over data so they don’t have to break through firewalls. They use urgency or scare tactics to bypass your usual good sense. They can even use AI to make a fake voice call sound like your loved one. Over-sharing by you on routine social media can expose personal details they exploit.

In my case, yes to all three. I felt a sense of urgency. I was already upset and not sleeping well. Posts on my social media offer information about my life.

It’s a sad fact that trusting to post on social media, believing what you read/see from others, and believing you recognize a familiar voice are all enough to clean out your entire savings. And cryptocurrency is the method used to take your money without any ability to trace it or recover it.

Fortunately, I lost no money, just time, though my self-esteem took a hit, but those intangible losses may be more valuable than money. Research demonstrates that the emotional cost of being hooked into a scam is significant, involving depression, self-criticism, and withdrawal. It takes support from others to recover, and a cognitive switch from self-blame to recognition that scammers are now extremely sophisticated. Software companies are constantly having to provide updates to all of us, which include new security patches. Still, you need time and self-forgiveness to recover.

What You Can Do to Protect Yourself

  1. When you encounter an email, text, or phone call that suddenly disturbs you, and you feel the need to respond immediately, don’t. Instead, pause. Even 15 minutes. Give yourself a chance to calm down. Question whether you’re thinking clearly.
  2. Verify the source of the email/phone call by using a recognized channel to do so. In my case, I could have keyed in the Microsoft.com website to investigate.
  3. Make sure you enable two-factor identification. Take advantage of other security measures like call blocking, credit freezes, protective software, online monitoring of accounts, and password management.
  4. If you’re using AI for ideas, or personal writing, etc., toggle off that website’s ability to save your material and use it for “training.”
  5. Protect yourself by reducing your reactions to stress, by doing your best to get decent sleep, and by choosing various ways of reducing your anxiety. A tired, worried, and anxious person is more vulnerable to being scammed.

Finally, if you have been the victim of a scam, gather all the information you can about it and report it to the FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3). They need that information to help you and others, and there’s a complaint form you can complete. They also offer a hotline for victims over age 60: DOJ Elder Justice Hotline, 1-833-372-8311.

And to add to feeling foolish, later that day, when I looked more closely at the photo of the FBI Badge sent to me to verify that my scammer was legit, it was a low-res image of David Duchovny’s FBI badge from The X-Files. Wow…

item.title: When No Psychiatric Diagnosis Seems to Fit
item.description:
Psychiatry

When No Psychiatric Diagnosis Seems to Fit

Tips to guide a discussion with your clinician when the diagnosis is elusive.

Posted September 8, 2026

Key points
  • It's common in treatment situations that a person's assigned diagnosis doesn't seem like a good fit.
  • Psychiatrists may tolerate this ambiguity more readily than clients.
  • A good conversation between client and clinician can help resolve some of the tension in this moment.
  • Very often, major improvements can still occur even with diagnostic uncertainty.

In medicine, we try very hard to turn the symptoms that people present with into a diagnosis that can help guide optimal treatment. It’s a system that sounds great but, in reality, often falls short. Despite the approximately 300 different mental health diagnoses contained within the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM) of Mental Disorders, it is extremely common that the clinical picture a patient/client describes doesn’t fit neatly into any of them. Many of us train for years trying to learn and understand the details and nuances of all these conditions, only to find out that our patients never got the memo and come to us with a mishmash of symptoms that aren’t supposed to go together and span multiple different categories, or none at all.

Clinicians newly out of training are often frustrated and disheartened by this situation. How come nobody looks like the textbook case I learned about? It can feel like trying to put the proverbial square peg in a round hole. Or maybe it is best just to list all the diagnoses that sorta apply, leaving someone with five or more different labels to wear.

Patients and families similarly can be unsettled with a poorly fitting diagnosis. For some people, psychiatric diagnoses are soulless constructions that do more harm than good, but for others they provide an organizing framework to understand their struggles, a community of others navigating similar waters, and a comforting reassurance that caring people know what this is and what to do about it. For these folks, the use of a coarsely applied diagnosis can easily create a feeling that something is amiss, and that they are not well understood.

I’ve come to appreciate that it is an important clinical moment when both a patient and their psychiatrist reach that point of acknowledging that none of the working diagnoses seem to fit a patient’s more complex profile. I’ve also come to learn that, quite frequently, the next step that the psychiatrist and patient want to take is exactly the opposite.

For the psychiatrist, this can often be a moment of acceptance and acknowledgement that the human brain is very complicated and the tidy little boxes we have constructed to try and capture all the variation that exists when it comes to mental health challenges are inadequate. He or she might decide that a particular diagnosis is good enough or that a more vague diagnosis (like all those “not otherwise specified” options) will work at least for the time being while trying to help a patient and their family overcome their most pressing concerns, regardless of what we call it. This point of acknowledgment may be particularly common if the psychiatrist is convinced that the assessment and diagnostic process has been sufficiently thorough and comprehensive.

For the patient and their family, however, this can be a moment to push the diagnostic and treatment process further, even if it means going into less-charted territory. Here, patients and families may voice that they think that “something else” is going on and request that “some tests” be performed, even if they don’t have a good idea what kind of test they want specifically or what the limits of these tests are. From the treatment side, this may be the moment of wanting to try a complementary or alternative treatment or something new and untested that they have seen online.

Complicating the picture on the part of the patient or family might be a reluctance to challenge the authority of the clinician or a worry that expressing doubt about a diagnosis is implying a lack of quality in the care. Most clinicians, however, are happy to have this discussion and won’t take offense if asked in a respectful way.

To help those who are questioning their diagnosis, here are a few suggestions to consider when having this discussion with your psychiatrist or other mental health professional.

  1. Be as specific as you can about your thoughts and concerns. Yes, people might feel a little sheepish admitting that the reason they are wondering about a specific test or diagnosis is that they saw something on TikTok, but having details can really help focus the discussion in a positive way.
  2. Think through both the potential positive and negative aspects of getting a new diagnosis. While some diagnoses can open the door for more services or accommodations, they can come at the price of increased stigma or, for diagnoses like borderline personality disorder, poorer medical care. Other diagnoses, like autism or bipolar disorder, can limit a person’s ability to, for example, join the military or fly a plane. I’ve been doing this long enough to see families push hard for a specific diagnosis when their child is younger, only to push hard to remove the diagnosis later. This can be difficult to justify.
  3. Focus on whether or not a diagnosis switch really changes anything. Sometimes a different diagnosis has major implications for things like medications; other times almost nothing different would happen from a practical standpoint. It may still be worthwhile to make a change, but sometimes patients and families are expecting much more from a diagnosis change than what actually occurs.

If after this discussion you still feel unsatisfied, it is fine to ask for a second opinion. These may be hard to find (and pay for), but often some avenues exist. If you do go for a second opinion, keep in mind that many self-declared experts in certain diagnoses tend to make that diagnosis a lot (remember the saying, "To a hammer, everything looks like a nail"), so these folks may not be your best source for an objective consultation. Relatedly, a new diagnosis doesn’t necessarily mean it is the correct one and that the original diagnosis is wrong. In mental health, there is just more subjectivity and clinical judgement that goes into making diagnoses compared to other areas of medicine.

Getting the most accurate diagnosis is important when it comes to mental health care. While it is unusual that the ordering of uncommon tests or procedures yields dramatic insights into a person’s diagnosis or treatment plan, exceptions do occur. In many instances, however, major improvements and gains can be made with a good comprehensive treatment approach even if the diagnosis is somewhat vague or uncertain.
